title: I came, I saw, I conquered
author: Suetonius

edition.name: Suetonius, De Vita Caesarum, Latin text of the Loeb Classical Library edition (J. C. Rolfe), as presented on LacusCurtius (Bill Thayer), which credits it as "Loeb Classical Library, 1913" and public domain

source_text: Pontico triumpho inter pompae fercula trium verborum praetulit titulum VENI·VIDI·VICI non acta belli significantem sicut ceteris, sed celeriter confecti notam.
excerpt_note: The last sentence of section 37.2. The edition prints the three words in capitals with raised dots, as on an inscription.

macrons.note: Macrons are editorial: added by Vocābula, not printed in the edition. Vowel quantities follow the app lexicon (Wheelock / DCC spellings) where the word is in it, and standard dictionary quantities otherwise.
uncertain: ācta: long ā (āctum), matching the app lexicon (agō, agere, ēgī, āctum).
cōnfectī: long ō before nf, matching the app lexicon (cōnficiō).
The capitals VĒNĪ·VĪDĪ·VĪCĪ keep the edition's inscription style; the macrons on them are editorial too.

translation: In the Pontic triumph, among the floats of the procession, he had a placard of three words carried ahead: I CAME · I SAW · I CONQUERED. Unlike the others, it did not describe the events of the war; it was a token of how quickly the war had been finished.
translation_note: cēterīs is compressed: "as (the placards did) for the others". The participle cōnfectī agrees with an understood bellī.

essay.t: In 47 BC Caesar fought King Pharnaces near Zela, a town in what is now northern Turkey (modern Zile).
Suetonius says he won within five days of arriving and within four hours of coming into the enemy's sight.
After the civil war Caesar celebrated four triumphs in a single month, with days between them, and a fifth later; one of them was for Pontus.
In that Pontic triumph, according to our passage, a placard with three words was carried among the floats.
Suetonius points out what made it unusual: other placards listed the events of a war, but this one advertised only its speed.
Plutarch tells a different story: Caesar wrote the three words in a letter to a friend at Rome named Amantius.
Plutarch also notes that in Latin the words share the same ending, which gives them an impressive brevity.
The name Amantius is odd, and the editor of a nineteenth-century English edition (Clough) suggested that the friend was Gaius Matius; this is a conjecture.
The two versions do not exclude each other: Caesar could have written the words in a letter and then reused them in Rome.
Neither author was a witness, though: Suetonius was born in AD 69, more than a century after Zela, and he relied freely on anecdote.
Still, the phrase is very likely Caesar's own wording in some form, since both writers attribute it to him and it fits the speed that Suetonius describes.
For a learner, the three verbs are a neat lesson: vēnī, vīdī and vīcī are perfect tenses of veniō, videō and vincō, each "I did it, and it is done".
The placard was propaganda in a literal sense: it told the crowd how to read the victory.

questions.q: According to Suetonius, what was unusual about the placard?
options: It described the speed of the victory rather than the events of the war
It was carried by Caesar himself

questions.q: Where does Plutarch say the three words appeared?
options: In a letter to a friend at Rome
In a speech to the Senate

questions.q: How long after coming into the enemy's sight did Suetonius say Caesar won?
